provenance.note: 1904.31 decides WHOSE 300 Log a case belongs on when the injured person is not a straightforward payroll employee. One test controls almost all of it: DAY-TO-DAY SUPERVISION. Payroll is not the test for temps and contractors — supervision is. 1904.31(b)(4) then requires the case be recorded exactly once, on one employer's log or the other's, never both.
provenance.verification_note: Verified against the eCFR text of 1904.31. Rule wording here is condensed for use as a controlled vocabulary — the substance and the sub-clause cites are checked, the phrasing is not verbatim.

payroll_categories.rule: All employees on your payroll are covered, whatever their category — labor, executive, hourly, salary, part-time, seasonal, or migrant. Their recordable cases go on your 300 Log regardless of who supervises them.

on_your_payroll.rule: The worker is on your payroll. You record their recordable injuries and illnesses, whatever their employment category and whoever supervises the work.

temporary_leased_or_supplied.rule: The worker comes from a temporary help service, employee leasing service or personnel supply service. You record their case if YOU supervise them on a day-to-day basis; otherwise the supplying company records it.

contractor_employee.rule: The worker is a contractor's employee working in your establishment. If the contractor provides day-to-day supervision, the contractor records the case. If YOU supervise the work day-to-day, you record it.

self_employed.rule: Self-employed individuals are not covered by the OSH Act or Part 1904 at all. Their injuries are not recorded by anyone — not by you, and not by a supplying employer.

owner_or_partner.rule: In a sole proprietorship or partnership, the owner or partners are not considered employees for recordkeeping purposes, so their injuries are not recorded on the 300 Log.

record_once.rule: The supplying service or contractor does NOT also record a case you record. Coordinate so each injury and illness is recorded exactly once — on your 300 Log if you provide day-to-day supervision, or on the other employer's if they do.
